Answer: - Item-to-item: Given current item, recommend similar items (product page "related items") - User-to-item: Given user profile, recommend personalized items (homepage feed) Explanation: Item-to-item: context-dependent, no user needed. User-to-item: personalized, requires user data. Both coexist in most systems.

•

Scenario 147. What is counterfactual evaluation for recommender systems?

AnswerMethodsExplanation

Answer: Estimate how a new policy would have performed using data collected by a different policy, without deploying. Methods: Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS), Doubly Robust estimation. Explanation: Existing recommendation data is biased by the current system. Counterfactual methods adjust for this bias. Enables safer offline evaluation before A/B testing.

•

Scenario 148. How does contextual information improve recommendations?

AnswerExampleExplanation

Answer: Context features: time of day, device, location, weather, mood, companion. Example: Recommend family movies on weekend evenings, quick recipes during weekday lunch. Explanation: Same user wants different items in different contexts. Context-aware models (factorization machines, contextual bandits) capture these dynamics.

•

Scenario 149. What is the inductive vs transductive distinction in recommendations?

AnswerTransductiveInductiveExplanation

Answer: - Transductive: Model specific users/items seen during training (can't handle new ones) - Inductive: Model generalizes to new users/items using features Explanation: Traditional CF is transductive. Feature-based/content-based is inductive. Modern GNN approaches can be inductive with node features.

•

Scenario 150. How would you design a production recommendation system from scratch?

AnswerExplanation

Answer:

  1. Data Collection: User interactions, item metadata, context
  2. Feature Engineering: User profile, item features, interaction features
  3. Candidate Generation: Multiple sources (CF, content, popularity, trending)
  4. Ranking: ML model combining all signals
  5. Re-ranking: Business rules, diversity, freshness
  6. Serving: Low-latency API with caching
  7. Evaluation: Offline metrics + A/B testing
  8. Monitoring: Engagement metrics, coverage, latency
  9. Feedback Loop: Continuous learning from new interactions
  10. Bias Mitigation: Position debiasing, fairness constraints

Explanation: Multi-stage pipeline, not a single model. Each stage optimizes different objectives. Continuous iteration and experimentation drive improvement.

Scenario 1. What is the difference between tokenization, stemming, and lemmatization?

AnswerTokenizationStemmingLemmatizationExplanation

Answer: - Tokenization: Splitting text into units (words, subwords, characters) - Stemming: Reducing to root form by rule-based suffix removal ("running" → "run", "better" → "bet") - Lemmatization: Reducing to dictionary base form using linguistic rules ("better" → "good", "running" → "run") Explanation: Lemmatization is more accurate but slower. Stemming is faster but can produce non-words. Both reduce vocabulary for simpler models.

•

Scenario 2. What is TF-IDF and how does it work?

AnswerTF (Term Frequency)IDF (Inverse Document Frequency)TF-IDFExplanation

Answer: - TF (Term Frequency): How often word appears in a document - IDF (Inverse Document Frequency): log(total_docs / docs_containing_word) — penalizes common words - TF-IDF: TF × IDF — high for distinctive words in a document Explanation: "the" has high TF but low IDF (appears everywhere). "quantum" has lower TF but high IDF (rare). TF-IDF captures word importance.

•

Scenario 3. What is the bag-of-words (BoW) limitation?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: 1. Loses word order ("dog bites man" = "man bites dog") 2. High dimensionality (vocabulary size) 3. Sparse vectors 4. No semantic understanding ("happy" and "joyful" are unrelated) Explanation: BoW is simple baseline. N-grams partially capture order. Word embeddings capture semantics. Transformers overcome all limitations.

•

Scenario 4. What are word embeddings and why are they better than BoW?

AnswerPropertiesExplanation

Answer: Dense vector representations where semantically similar words are close in vector space. Properties: - "king" - "man" + "woman" ≈ "queen" - Similar words have high cosine similarity - Fixed-size dense vectors (100-300 dimensions) Explanation: Capture semantic and syntactic relationships. Pre-trained (Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText) or learned end-to-end. Dramatically improve NLP model performance.

•

Scenario 5. What is the difference between Word2Vec and GloVe?

AnswerWord2VecGloVeExplanation

Answer: - Word2Vec: Predictive model (Skip-gram: predict context from word. CBOW: predict word from context). Learns from local windows. - GloVe: Count-based model — factorizes global co-occurrence matrix. Captures global statistics. Explanation: Both produce similar quality embeddings. Word2Vec: local context windows. GloVe: global corpus statistics. FastText extends Word2Vec with subword (character n-gram) embeddings.

•

Scenario 6. What is the advantage of FastText over Word2Vec?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: FastText represents words as sum of character n-gram embeddings, enabling: 1. Handle out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words 2. Better representations for rare words 3. Morphological understanding ("unhappy" shares subwords with "happy") Explanation: Word2Vec assigns one vector per word — OOV words get nothing. FastText: even unseen words have representations based on character n-grams.

•

Scenario 7. How do you handle text preprocessing for NLP?

AnswerExplanation

Answer:

import re
text = text.lower()                          # Lowercase
text = re.sub(r'[^a-zA-Z\s]', '', text)    # Remove punctuation
text = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text).strip()    # Normalize whitespace
# Tokenize
tokens = text.split()
# Remove stopwords
tokens = [t for t in tokens if t not in stop_words]
# Lemmatize
tokens = [lemmatizer.lemmatize(t) for t in tokens]

Explanation: Preprocessing depends on task. Sentiment analysis: keep punctuation (!?), negation ("not"). Deep learning: often minimal preprocessing.

•

Scenario 8. When should you NOT remove stop words?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: 1. Sentiment analysis ("not good" → removing "not" changes meaning) 2. Phrase detection ("United States" needs both words) 3. Deep learning models (handle context themselves) 4. Question answering ("what", "who", "how" are stop words but critical) Explanation: Stop word removal is a heuristic from IR era. Modern models (BERT, transformers) work better with full text.

•

Scenario 9. What is text classification and what are the common approaches?

AnswerTraditional MLDeep LearningTransfer LearningZero-shotExplanation

Answer: - Traditional ML: TF-IDF + Logistic Regression/SVM/Naive Bayes - Deep Learning: CNN/LSTM/Transformer on word embeddings - Transfer Learning: Fine-tune BERT/RoBERTa - Zero-shot: GPT/LLM with prompting Explanation: TF-IDF + Logistic Regression is a strong baseline. Fine-tuned BERT is state-of-the-art for most tasks. Choose based on data size and compute budget.

•

Scenario 10. Why is Naive Bayes effective for text classification despite its strong independence assumption?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Despite assuming feature independence (words are independent given class), Naive Bayes works because: 1. Classification only needs relative probabilities (ranking) 2. High dimensionality makes independence a reasonable approximation 3. Very robust to irrelevant features 4. Handles small datasets well Explanation: Naive Bayes often outperforms complex models on small text datasets. Fast training and prediction. Good first baseline.

•

Scenario 11. What is the difference between Multinomial and Bernoulli Naive Bayes for text?

AnswerMultinomialBernoulliExplanation

Answer: - Multinomial: Uses word counts/frequencies. Works with TF-IDF. Better for longer documents. - Bernoulli: Uses binary presence/absence. Considers absence of words. Better for short texts. Explanation: Multinomial: "word appearing 5 times is different from 1 time." Bernoulli: "word present or not." Multinomial handles document length better.

•

Scenario 12. What is sentiment analysis and what are its challenges?

AnswerChallengesExplanation

Answer: Determining emotional tone (positive/negative/neutral) from text. Challenges: 1. Sarcasm/irony ("Oh great, another delay!") 2. Negation ("not bad" = positive) 3. Domain-specific sentiment ("sick" = positive in slang) 4. Comparative sentiment ("better than X but worse than Y") 5. Aspect-level sentiment (food: positive, service: negative) Explanation: Lexicon-based (dictionary of sentiment words) or ML-based. Modern: fine-tuned transformers. Aspect-based sentiment analysis is more granular.

•

Scenario 13. What is Named Entity Recognition (NER)?

AnswerExampleExplanation

Answer: Identifying and classifying named entities in text: persons, organizations, locations, dates, quantities, etc. Example: "[Google]_ORG announced at [I/O]_EVENT that [Sundar Pichai]_PERSON will present [June 15]_DATE." Explanation: Approaches: rule-based, CRF (Conditional Random Fields), BiLSTM-CRF, fine-tuned BERT. spaCy provides pre-trained NER models.

•

Scenario 14. What is text similarity and how do you measure it?

AnswerCosine similarity on TF-IDFWord Mover's DistanceSentence embeddingsEdit distanceExplanation

Answer: 1. Cosine similarity on TF-IDF: Simple, no semantics 2. Word Mover's Distance: Based on word embedding distances 3. Sentence embeddings: SBERT (Sentence-BERT) cosine similarity 4. Edit distance: Character-level similarity (Levenshtein) Explanation: TF-IDF: "buy car" and "purchase automobile" = dissimilar. Sentence embeddings: similar because semantically equivalent.

•

Scenario 15. What is the difference between word-level and subword tokenization?

AnswerWord-levelSubwordMethodsExplanation

Answer: - Word-level: "unhappiness" → ["unhappiness"] — OOV problem for rare words - Subword: "unhappiness" → ["un", "happi", "ness"] — handles any word, smaller vocabulary - Methods: BPE (Byte Pair Encoding), WordPiece, SentencePiece Explanation: Modern models (BERT, GPT) use subword tokenization. Balances vocabulary size with morphological coverage. No OOV problem.

•

Scenario 16. What is topic modeling and how does LDA work?

AnswerLDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation)Explanation

Answer: Discovering abstract topics from a collection of documents. LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation): - Each document = mixture of topics - Each topic = distribution over words - Generative model: document → topics → words Explanation: Unsupervised. Learn: topic-word distributions and document-topic distributions. Hyperparameters: number of topics, alpha (document-topic density), beta (topic-word density).

•

Scenario 17. How do you evaluate topic models?

AnswerCoherence scorePerplexityHuman evaluationExplanation

Answer: 1. Coherence score: Semantic similarity of top words in each topic (higher = more interpretable) 2. Perplexity: How well model predicts held-out documents (lower = better fit) 3. Human evaluation: Do topics make sense to domain experts? Explanation: Coherence and perplexity can disagree. Coherence better correlates with human judgment. Try different topic counts, pick highest coherence.

•

Scenario 18. What is text summarization?

AnswerExtractiveAbstractiveExplanation

Answer: - Extractive: Select important sentences from original text (TextRank, BERT-based selection) - Abstractive: Generate new sentences that capture key information (Seq2Seq, T5, BART, GPT) Explanation: Extractive: guaranteed faithful, but may sound choppy. Abstractive: more fluent but may hallucinate. Modern systems increasingly abstractive.

•

Scenario 19. What is the sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) model?

AnswerApplicationsExplanation

Answer: Encoder-decoder architecture: encoder reads input sequence → hidden state → decoder generates output sequence. Applications: Translation, summarization, question answering. Explanation: Encoder: input → context vector. Decoder: context vector → output. Attention mechanism improves by allowing decoder to focus on specific input parts.

•

Scenario 20. What is attention mechanism in NLP?

AnswerFormulaExplanation

Answer: Allows model to dynamically focus on relevant parts of the input when generating each output token. Formula: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / √d) × V Explanation: Without attention: entire input compressed to single vector (bottleneck). With attention: decoder selects relevant input positions for each output step. Foundation of Transformers.

•

Scenario 21. What is the Transformer architecture?

AnswerComponentsExplanation

Answer: Self-attention-based architecture replacing RNNs. Processes all tokens in parallel. Components: Multi-head self-attention, feed-forward layers, positional encoding, layer normalization. Explanation: No recurrence → parallelizable, efficient. Self-attention captures long-range dependencies. Base of BERT, GPT, T5, and all modern NLP.

•

Scenario 22. What is BERT and how does it work?

AnswerUsageExplanation

Answer: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Pre-trained on: 1. Masked Language Model (MLM): predict masked words 2. Next Sentence Prediction (NSP): predict if sentence B follows A Usage: Fine-tune on downstream tasks (classification, NER, QA). Explanation: Bidirectional: considers context from both left and right (unlike GPT which is left-to-right). State-of-the-art for understanding tasks. Not for text generation.

•

Scenario 23. What is the difference between BERT and GPT?

AnswerBERTGPTExplanation

Answer: - BERT: Encoder-only, bidirectional, good for understanding (classification, NER, QA) - GPT: Decoder-only, left-to-right, good for generation (text completion, summarization) Explanation: BERT sees full context for each token. GPT sees only previous tokens (autoregressive). GPT-3/4 is massive and can do few-shot learning.

•

Scenario 24. How do you fine-tune BERT for text classification?

AnswerExplanation

Answer:

from transformers import BertForSequenceClassification, Trainer

model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    'bert-base-uncased', num_labels=3
)
trainer = Trainer(
    model=model,
    train_dataset=train_dataset,
    eval_dataset=eval_dataset,
    args=training_args
)
trainer.train()

Explanation: Add classification head on [CLS] token embedding. Fine-tune all layers with small learning rate (2e-5). Few epochs (2-4) sufficient. Dramatically better than training from scratch.

•

Scenario 25. What is transfer learning in NLP?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Pre-train large language model on massive text corpus (unsupervised), then fine-tune on specific task with smaller labeled dataset.

Pre-train: BERT on Wikipedia/BookCorpus (millions of texts)
Fine-tune: Your sentiment dataset (1000 labeled examples)

Explanation: Pre-training learns general language understanding. Fine-tuning adapts to specific task. Enables high performance with limited labeled data.

•

Scenario 26. What is the difference between character-level, word-level, and subword-level models?

AnswerCharacterWordSubwordExplanation

Answer: - Character: Smallest vocabulary, handles any text, but sequences very long - Word: Natural units, but large vocabulary and OOV problem - Subword: Balance — small vocabulary, handles OOV, moderate sequence length Explanation: Modern NLP: subword (BPE, WordPiece). Character-level: useful for morphologically rich languages or noisy text (typos).

•

Scenario 27. What is Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging?

AnswerExampleMethodsExplanation

Answer: Assigning grammatical categories (noun, verb, adjective, etc.) to each word. Example: "The/DET cat/NOUN sat/VERB on/ADP the/DET mat/NOUN" Methods: Rule-based, HMM, CRF, BiLSTM, BERT. Explanation: Foundational NLP task. Helps disambiguation ("bank" = river bank vs financial bank). Modern models do POS implicitly.

•

Scenario 28. What is dependency parsing?

AnswerExampleExplanation

Answer: Analyzing grammatical structure by finding relationships between words (head-dependent pairs). Example: "The cat sat on the mat" → sat is root, cat→sat (nsubj), mat→sat (obl). Explanation: Captures syntactic structure. Used for relation extraction, question answering, information extraction. spaCy provides fast dependency parsing.

•

Scenario 29. What is word sense disambiguation?

AnswerExampleExplanation

Answer: Determining which meaning of a word is used in context. Example: "bank": - "River bank" → geographical feature - "Bank account" → financial institution Explanation: Context determines meaning. BERT-style models handle this implicitly through contextual embeddings (same word, different vectors in different contexts).

•

Scenario 30. What is the difference between rule-based and ML-based NLP?

AnswerRule-basedML-basedExplanation

Answer: - Rule-based: Hand-crafted patterns and rules (regex, grammars). Precise for known patterns, brittle for variations. - ML-based: Learn patterns from data. More flexible, handle variations, need labeled data. Explanation: Production systems often combine both: ML for broad coverage, rules for critical patterns (phone numbers, emails, specific formats).

•

Scenario 31. What is information extraction?

AnswerNERRelation extractionEvent extractionCoreference resolutionExplanation

Answer: Extracting structured information from unstructured text: 1. NER: Entity identification 2. Relation extraction: Relationships between entities 3. Event extraction: What happened, when, where, to whom 4. Coreference resolution: "he" refers to "John" Explanation: Transforms text into structured data (knowledge base entries, database records). Pipeline: NER → relation extraction → knowledge graph.

•

Scenario 32. How do you handle multi-language NLP?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: 1. Language detection first (langdetect, fasttext) 2. Language-specific models/preprocessing 3. Multilingual models: mBERT, XLM-R (100+ languages) 4. Machine translation → process in target language Explanation: Multilingual models: train once, deploy for many languages. Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer: fine-tune on English, test on other languages.

•

Scenario 33. What is text normalization?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Standardizing text variations: 1. Lowercasing: "Apple" → "apple" 2. Unicode normalization: "café" → "cafe" 3. Contractions: "don't" → "do not" 4. Number normalization: "1st" → "first" 5. Abbreviation expansion: "NYC" → "New York City" Explanation: Reduces vocabulary and variation. Domain-specific: medical abbreviations, social media slang. Too aggressive normalization loses information.

•

Scenario 34. What is the cosine similarity for text comparison?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: cosine(A, B) = (A · B) / (||A|| × ||B||). Measures angle between vectors, not magnitude. - Range: [-1, 1] (for TF-IDF: [0, 1]) - 1 = identical direction, 0 = orthogonal, -1 = opposite Explanation: Preferred over Euclidean for text because it's magnitude-invariant — a document twice as long has similar cosine but very different Euclidean distance.

•

Scenario 35. What is N-gram language modeling?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Probabilities of word sequences using conditional probability: P(w_n | w_{n-1}, ..., w_{n-N+1}). - Unigram: P(word) independent - Bigram: P(word | previous_word) - Trigram: P(word | two_previous_words) Explanation: Simple, interpretable. Limited context window. Smoothing needed for unseen n-grams (Laplace, Kneser-Ney). Replaced by neural language models.

•

Scenario 36. What is perplexity in language modeling?

AnswerFormulaInterpretationExplanation

Answer: Measures how well a language model predicts text. Lower = better. Formula: PP = exp(-1/N × Σ log P(w_i)) Interpretation: Perplexity = 100 means the model is as confused as choosing uniformly from 100 words. Explanation: Used to compare language models. Not directly comparable across different tokenizations/vocabularies.

•

Scenario 37. What is the SpaCy vs NLTK comparison?

AnswerNLTKSpaCyExplanation

Answer: - NLTK: Academic, educational, many algorithms, slower, more flexibility - SpaCy: Production-ready, fast, opinionated (one algorithm per task), pre-trained pipelines Explanation: Use spaCy for production NLP pipelines (NER, POS, parsing). NLTK for learning and experimentation. Hugging Face Transformers for state-of-the-art models.

•

Scenario 38. What is document similarity search?

AnswerApproachesExplanation

Answer: Finding documents most similar to a query or reference document. Approaches: 1. TF-IDF + cosine similarity 2. BM25 (improved TF-IDF for information retrieval) 3. Dense retrieval (BERT-based embeddings + ANN search) 4. Hybrid: BM25 + dense retrieval Explanation: BM25 is the standard baseline. Dense retrieval captures semantics. Production: embed documents offline, ANN search at query time.

•

Scenario 39. What is text augmentation for NLP?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: 1. Synonym replacement (WordNet or embedding similarity) 2. Random insertion/deletion/swap 3. Back-translation (English → French → English) 4. Contextual augmentation (use BERT to fill masked words) 5. Paraphrasing with LLMs Explanation: Increases training data diversity. Back-translation most reliable. Be careful: augmentation shouldn't change label.

•

Scenario 40. What is the BM25 scoring function?

Answer: Best Matching 25 — TF-IDF variant with: 1. Term frequency saturation (diminishing returns for repeated words) 2. Document length normalization 3. IDF weighting Formula includes k1, b parameters controlling saturation and length normalization. Explanation:** Default scoring in Elasticsearch, Solr. Strong baseline for search. Often used as first-stage retrieval before neural re-ranking.

•

Scenario 41. What is the difference between semantic similarity and lexical similarity?

AnswerLexicalSemanticExplanation

Answer: - Lexical: Based on exact word/character overlap ("buy car" vs "buy car" = high) - Semantic: Based on meaning ("buy car" vs "purchase automobile" = high) Explanation: BLEU, ROUGE measure lexical overlap. BERTScore measures semantic similarity. Semantic similarity captures paraphrases and synonyms.

•

Scenario 42. How do you handle noisy text data (social media, OCR, etc.)?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: 1. Spell correction (SymSpell, pyspellchecker) 2. Custom normalization rules (slang dictionary) 3. Character-level or subword models (robust to misspellings) 4. Data augmentation with noise injection 5. Pre-training on similar noisy data Explanation: "Luv dis movie sooo much!!!" → standard models struggle. Character-level models and pre-training on Twitter data help.

•

Scenario 43. What is Regular Expression (regex) usage in NLP?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Pattern matching for extracting structured information from text:

import re
# Extract dates
dates = re.findall(r'\d{1,2}/\d{1,2}/\d{2,4}', text)
# Extract emails
emails = re.findall(r'[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+', text)
# Extract phone numbers
phones = re.findall(r'\(?\d{3}\)?[-.\s]?\d{3}[-.\s]?\d{4}', text)

Explanation: Essential for data extraction, preprocessing, and validation. Rule-based NLP for well-defined patterns. Use named groups for clarity.

•

Scenario 44. What is the difference between extractive and abstractive question answering?

AnswerExtractiveAbstractiveRetrieval-augmentedExplanation

Answer: - Extractive: Find answer span in given context (BERT-based: SQuAD-style) - Abstractive: Generate answer text, possibly not in the context (GPT, T5) - Retrieval-augmented: Retrieve relevant documents, then extract/generate answer (RAG) Explanation: Extractive: faithful but limited to context. Abstractive: flexible but may hallucinate. RAG combines retrieval quality with generation flexibility.

•

Scenario 45. What is the Jaccard similarity for text?

AnswerExampleExplanation

Answer: |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B| — intersection over union of word sets. Example: A = {the, cat, sat}, B = {the, dog, sat} → Jaccard = 2/4 = 0.5 Explanation: Simple but ignores word frequency and order. Useful for near-duplicate detection. MinHash provides efficient approximation for large-scale.

•

Scenario 46. What is cross-encoder vs bi-encoder for text matching?

AnswerBi-encoderCross-encoderExplanation

Answer: - Bi-encoder: Encode query and document separately, compare embeddings (fast, independent) - Cross-encoder: Encode query-document pair jointly (more accurate, but can't pre-compute) Explanation: Bi-encoder: pre-compute document embeddings, real-time query embedding + ANN. Cross-encoder: re-rank top candidates from bi-encoder. Two-stage pipeline is common.

•

Scenario 47. What is active learning for text annotation?

AnswerStrategiesExplanation

Answer: Select the most informative unlabeled samples for human annotation, rather than random selection. Strategies: 1. Uncertainty sampling (model is least confident) 2. Query by committee (models disagree) 3. Diversity sampling (maximize coverage) Explanation: Reduces annotation cost by 50-80%. Iterative: model trains → selects → human labels → retrain. Critical for NLP where labeling is expensive.

•

Scenario 48. What is the difference between keyword extraction and keyphrase extraction?

AnswerKeywordKeyphraseMethodsExplanation

Answer: - Keyword: Single important words ("machine", "learning") - Keyphrase: Multi-word expressions ("machine learning", "natural language processing") Methods: TF-IDF, TextRank, YAKE, KeyBERT. Explanation: Keyphrases are more informative. KeyBERT uses BERT embeddings to find phrases most similar to the document embedding.

•

Scenario 49. How do you build a text classification pipeline from scratch?

AnswerExplanation

Answer:

from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

pipe = Pipeline([
    ('tfidf', TfidfVectorizer(
        max_features=10000, ngram_range=(1,2),
        min_df=5, max_df=0.95
    )),
    ('clf', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
])
pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(pipe.score(X_test, y_test))

Explanation: Strong baseline. Often achieves 85-95% of BERT performance with 100x less compute. Add: cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, error analysis.

•

Scenario 50. What are the key considerations when deploying NLP models in production?

AnswerLatencyModel sizePreprocessing consistencyEdge casesMonitoring

Answer: 1. Latency: Tokenization + inference time (BERT is slow, distilled models faster) 2. Model size: BERT-base = 440MB, DistilBERT = 260MB 3. Preprocessing consistency: Same tokenizer in train and serve 4. Edge cases: Empty text, very long text, unsupported languages 5. Monitoring: Drift in text distribution, new vocabulary 6. Updates: Retrain as language evolves Explanation: Distillation, quantization, ONNX export for production speed. Cache frequent predictions. Batch inference for offline tasks.

•

Scenario 51. What is a perceptron and how does it relate to logistic regression?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: A perceptron is a single neuron: y = activation(w·x + b). With sigmoid activation, it's equivalent to logistic regression. Explanation: Perceptron: simplest neural unit. Can only learn linearly separable patterns. Multi-layer perceptron (MLP) overcomes this by stacking layers with non-linear activations.

•

Scenario 52. What is the role of activation functions?

AnswerCommon activationsReLUSigmoidTanhSoftmax

Answer: Introduce non-linearity. Without activations, stacking layers is just one big linear transformation (matrix multiplication). Common activations: - ReLU: max(0, x) — simple, fast, most popular - Sigmoid: 1/(1+e^-x) — outputs (0,1), vanishing gradients - Tanh: (e^x - e^-x)/(e^x + e^-x) — outputs (-1,1) - Softmax: Multi-class output probabilities Explanation: ReLU is default for hidden layers. Sigmoid for binary output. Softmax for multi-class output.

•

Scenario 53. What is the vanishing gradient problem?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: In deep networks with sigmoid/tanh, gradients become exponentially small during backpropagation, making early layers learn extremely slowly. Explanation: Sigmoid derivative max = 0.25. Multiplying through many layers: 0.25^20 ≈ 10^-12. Solutions: ReLU, batch normalization, residual connections, better initialization (He/Xavier).

•

Scenario 54. What is the exploding gradient problem?

AnswerSolutionsExplanation

Answer: Gradients become exponentially large, causing weight updates to overflow. Solutions: 1. Gradient clipping: cap gradient magnitude 2. Proper initialization (Xavier/He) 3. Batch normalization 4. Learning rate reduction Explanation: Common in RNNs. Gradient clipping: if ||gradient|| > threshold, scale down to threshold. Simple and effective.

•

Scenario 55. What is backpropagation?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Algorithm to compute gradients of loss with respect to all weights by applying chain rule from output to input layer.

∂Loss/∂w = ∂Loss/∂output × ∂output/∂hidden × ∂hidden/∂w

Explanation: Forward pass: compute predictions. Backward pass: compute gradients. Update weights: w = w - lr × gradient. Foundation of neural network training.

•

Scenario 56. What is the difference between batch, mini-batch, and stochastic gradient descent?

AnswerBatch GDMini-batch GDStochastic GDExplanation

Answer: - Batch GD: Use entire dataset for each update (stable, slow) - Mini-batch GD: Use subset (32-256 samples) per update (balanced) - Stochastic GD: Use 1 sample per update (noisy, fast) Explanation: Mini-batch is standard practice. Batch size affects: convergence speed, generalization, memory usage. Larger batch → faster but may generalize worse.

•

Scenario 57. What are common optimizers and when to use each?

AnswerSGD + MomentumAdamAdamWRMSpropExplanation

Answer: - SGD + Momentum: Simple, good generalization, needs tuning - Adam: Adaptive learning rates, fast convergence, default choice - AdamW: Adam with decoupled weight decay (better regularization) - RMSprop: Good for RNNs Explanation: Adam: maintains per-parameter learning rates based on gradient history. Converges faster than SGD. AdamW: fixes weight decay inconsistency in Adam.

•

Scenario 58. What is the learning rate and why is it the most important hyperparameter?

AnswerToo highToo lowJust rightExplanation

Answer: Controls step size of weight updates: w_new = w_old - lr × gradient. - Too high: Overshoots, unstable/diverges - Too low: Very slow convergence, may get stuck - Just right: Fast convergence to good minimum Explanation: Use learning rate finder (increase lr exponentially, plot loss). Typically 1e-5 to 1e-1. Cosine annealing or warmup schedules improve training.

•

Scenario 59. What is dropout and how does it prevent overfitting?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Randomly sets a fraction of neuron outputs to zero during training. Forces network to learn redundant representations.

nn.Dropout(p=0.5)  # Drop 50% of neurons randomly each forward pass

Explanation: Ensemble effect: each forward pass uses a different subnetwork. At inference: use all neurons, scale by (1-p). Typical: 0.1-0.5. Not used in batch norm layers typically.

•

Scenario 60. What is batch normalization and why does it help?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Normalizes layer inputs to zero mean and unit variance within each mini-batch, then applies learned scale and shift.

BN(x) = γ × (x - μ_batch) / σ_batch + β

Explanation: Benefits: faster training, higher learning rates, slight regularization, reduces internal covariate shift. Applied before or after activation (debate). Uses running statistics at inference.

•

Scenario 61. What is the difference between L1 and L2 regularization in neural networks?

AnswerL1 (Lasso)L2 (Weight decay)Explanation

Answer: - L1 (Lasso): Adds |w| to loss → drives weights to exactly zero (sparse) - L2 (Weight decay): Adds w² to loss → keeps weights small but non-zero Explanation: L2 is more common in neural networks (weight_decay parameter in optimizers). L1 leads to sparse networks. Both prevent overfitting by penalizing large weights.

•

Scenario 62. What is Xavier (Glorot) initialization?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Initializes weights from distribution with variance = 2 / (fan_in + fan_out).

# Normal: W ~ N(0, sqrt(2/(n_in + n_out)))
# Uniform: W ~ U(-sqrt(6/(n_in + n_out)), sqrt(6/(n_in + n_out)))

Explanation: Designed for sigmoid/tanh activations. Keeps variance stable across layers. He initialization (variance = 2/fan_in) for ReLU activations.

•

Scenario 63. What is a loss function and how do you choose one?

AnswerBinary classificationMulti-class classificationRegressionRankingExplanation

Answer: - Binary classification: Binary cross-entropy (BCELoss) - Multi-class classification: Cross-entropy loss (softmax + NLL) - Regression: MSE, MAE, Huber loss - Ranking: Margin loss, triplet loss Explanation: Loss function defines what the network optimizes. Must match the task. Custom losses for specific business needs (e.g., asymmetric loss for imbalanced data).

•

Scenario 64. What is the softmax function?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Converts raw scores (logits) to probabilities that sum to 1.

softmax(z_i) = exp(z_i) / Σ exp(z_j)

Explanation: Used as output layer for multi-class classification. Amplifies differences between logits. Temperature parameter T: softmax(z/T) — lower T → sharper distribution.

•

Scenario 65. What is early stopping for neural networks?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Stop training when validation loss stops improving for a specified number of epochs (patience).

early_stop = EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=10, 
                           restore_best_weights=True)

Explanation: Prevents overfitting without explicit regularization. Training loss continues to decrease while validation loss increases → overfitting point. Restore best weights from the epoch with lowest validation loss.

•

Scenario 66. What is the universal approximation theorem?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: A neural network with a single hidden layer of sufficient width can approximate any continuous function to arbitrary accuracy. Explanation: Guarantees existence, not learnability. Doesn't tell you: how many neurons, how to train, or if gradient descent will find the solution. Deep networks are more efficient approximators than wide ones.

•

Scenario 67. What is transfer learning in neural networks?

AnswerStrategiesFeature extractionFine-tuningProgressive unfreezingExplanation

Answer: Using a pre-trained network (trained on large dataset) and adapting it to a new task. Strategies: 1. Feature extraction: Freeze pre-trained layers, train new head 2. Fine-tuning: Unfreeze and train all layers with small lr 3. Progressive unfreezing: Gradually unfreeze layers Explanation: ImageNet-trained CNN for medical imaging. BERT for domain-specific NLP. Saves compute and works with small datasets.

•

Scenario 68. What is the difference between fine-tuning and feature extraction?

AnswerFeature extractionFine-tuningExplanation

Answer: - Feature extraction: Pre-trained layers frozen. Only new layers train. Faster, less overfitting risk. - Fine-tuning: All layers trainable (small lr for pre-trained, larger for new). Better adaptation but risk overfitting on small data. Explanation: Start with feature extraction. If performance insufficient, fine-tune with small lr (1e-5 to 1e-4). Freeze early layers (generic features) more aggressively.

•

Scenario 69. What is a residual connection (skip connection)?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Adds the input of a layer directly to its output: output = F(x) + x. Explanation: Enables training of very deep networks (100+ layers). Gradient flows directly through skip connection. Network only needs to learn the residual F(x) = desired_output - x. Foundation of ResNet.

•

Scenario 70. What is a convolutional layer and how does it differ from dense layers?

AnswerDense (fully connected)ConvolutionalExplanation

Answer: - Dense (fully connected): Each neuron connects to ALL inputs. Parameters: n_in × n_out. - Convolutional: Small filter slides across input. Parameter sharing, local connectivity. Parameters: filter_size × filters. Explanation: CNN: translation invariant, much fewer parameters for spatial data (images). Dense: no spatial structure assumed. CNN for images/sequences, Dense for tabular.

•

Scenario 71. When would you use a neural network vs traditional ML for tabular data?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Traditional ML (XGBoost, Random Forest) is generally better for tabular data because: 1. Handles heterogeneous features naturally 2. Fewer hyperparameters to tune 3. Less data needed 4. Handles missing values natively 5. More interpretable Explanation: Neural nets for tabular: TabNet, FT-Transformer sometimes match, rarely beat XGBoost. Use neural nets when: massive data, multimodal, representation learning needed.

•

Scenario 72. What is the role of the bias term in neural networks?

Answery = w×x + bExplanation

Answer: Allows the activation function to shift left/right, enabling the neuron to fit data that doesn't pass through the origin. y = w×x + b — b shifts the activation function. Explanation: Without bias: line must pass through origin. With bias: can fit any intercept. Each neuron has its own bias. Small but important for flexibility.

•

Scenario 73. What is gradient checking and why is it useful?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Verifying backpropagation correctness by comparing analytical gradients to numerical gradients:

∂L/∂w ≈ [L(w+ε) - L(w-ε)] / (2ε)

Explanation: Compare numerical approximation to backprop gradient. If they differ significantly (relative error > 1e-5), backprop implementation is buggy. Essential when implementing custom layers/losses.

•

Scenario 74. What is the dying ReLU problem?

AnswerCausesSolutionsExplanation

Answer: Neurons with ReLU that output 0 for all inputs. Their gradients are 0, so they never update (permanently dead). Causes: Large negative bias or very large learning rate. Solutions: Leaky ReLU (small slope for negative), PReLU (learnable slope), ELU, GELU. Explanation: Leaky ReLU: max(0.01x, x). GELU: smooth approximation used in BERT/GPT. Dying ReLU rarely a problem with He init + reasonable lr.

•

Scenario 75. What is data parallelism vs model parallelism?

AnswerData parallelismModel parallelismExplanation

Answer: - Data parallelism: Same model replicated on multiple GPUs, each processes different data batch. Gradients averaged. - Model parallelism: Different parts of model on different GPUs. For models too large for one GPU. Explanation: Data parallelism: easy, scales batch size. Model parallelism: complex, for very large models (GPT-3+). Most common: data parallelism with PyTorch DDP.

•

Scenario 76. What is mixed precision training?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Use FP16 (half precision) for forward/backward pass and FP32 for weight updates. 2× memory savings, faster compute.

scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler()
with torch.cuda.amp.autocast():
    output = model(input)
    loss = criterion(output, target)
scaler.scale(loss).backward()
scaler.step(optimizer)

Explanation: Modern GPUs have dedicated FP16 hardware (Tensor Cores). Loss scaling prevents underflow. Minimal accuracy impact.

•

Scenario 77. What is knowledge distillation?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Training a small "student" model to mimic a large "teacher" model's outputs (soft labels/ logits).

Student loss = α × CrossEntropy(student, true_labels) + 
               (1-α) × KL_Divergence(student_logits/T, teacher_logits/T)

Explanation: Teacher's soft probabilities contain richer information than hard labels (dark knowledge). DistilBERT: 40% smaller, 60% faster, 97% of BERT's performance.

•

Scenario 78. What is the difference between epoch, iteration, and batch?

AnswerEpochBatch (mini-batch)IterationExampleExplanation

Answer: - Epoch: One complete pass through entire training dataset - Batch (mini-batch): Subset of data processed together (e.g., 32 samples) - Iteration: One batch forward + backward pass Example: 1000 samples, batch=100 → 10 iterations per epoch. Explanation: Typically train 10-100+ epochs. Monitor validation metrics per epoch. Too many epochs → overfitting.

•

Scenario 79. What is weight decay and how does it differ from L2 regularization?

AnswerL2 regularizationWeight decayExplanation

Answer: Both penalize large weights but differ in implementation with adaptive optimizers: - L2 regularization: Adds λ||w||² to loss (gradient: 2λw added to gradient) - Weight decay: Directly shrinks weights: w = w - lr×decay×w (independent of gradient) Explanation: With SGD: equivalent. With Adam: L2 regularization is incorrect because adaptive lr scales the penalty. AdamW implements proper weight decay.

•

Scenario 80. What is a learning rate warmup?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Start with very low learning rate, gradually increase to target lr over first few hundred/thousand steps. Explanation: Prevents early instability when moving statistics (Adam) are inaccurate. Common: linear warmup for 5-10% of training. Then decay (cosine, linear). Essential for Transformers.

•

Scenario 81. What is the difference between online learning and batch learning?

AnswerBatchOnlineExplanation

Answer: - Batch: Train on entire dataset at once, retrain periodically - Online: Update model with each new data point, continuous learning Explanation: Online: adaptable, handles drift, memory-efficient. Batch: more stable, thorough optimization. SGD enables online learning naturally. Production: mini-batch + periodic retraining.

•

Scenario 82. What is the effect of batch size on training?

AnswerSmall batch (16-32)Large batch (256-4096)Explanation

Answer: - Small batch (16-32): Noisy gradients → regularization effect, better generalization, slower - Large batch (256-4096): Smoother gradients → faster computation, may generalize worse Explanation: Large batch: need learning rate scaling (linear scaling rule). Large batch may converge to sharp minima (poor generalization). Small batch finds flatter minima.

•

Scenario 83. What are embeddings in neural networks?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Learnable dense vector representations for discrete entities (words, categories, users, items).

embedding = nn.Embedding(num_categories=1000, embedding_dim=64)
# Input: category index → Output: 64-dim vector

Explanation: Replace one-hot encoding (sparse, high-dim) with dense, low-dim learned representations. Captures similarity — similar entities have similar embeddings.

•

Scenario 84. What is the attention mechanism intuitively?

AnswerIntuitionExplanation

Answer: Weighted sum of values, where weights are determined by compatibility between query and keys.

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / √d_k) V

Intuition: "Given what I'm looking for (Q), how relevant is each piece of information (K)? Weight the content (V) accordingly." Explanation: Self-attention: Q, K, V all come from same input. Cross-attention: Q from one source, K/V from another. Multi-head: multiple attention patterns in parallel.

•

Scenario 85. What is the difference between self-attention and cross-attention?

AnswerSelf-attentionCross-attentionExplanation

Answer: - Self-attention: Q, K, V from same sequence — each token attends to all other tokens in same sequence - Cross-attention: Q from one sequence, K/V from another — decoder attends to encoder outputs Explanation: Self-attention in BERT: each word relates to all other words. Cross-attention in translation: output word attends to input words.

•

Scenario 86. What is layer normalization?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Normalizes across features for each sample (not across batch like batch norm).

LN(x) = γ × (x - μ_features) / σ_features + β

Explanation: Batch norm depends on batch statistics → problematic for small batches and RNNs/Transformers. Layer norm: independent of batch → used in Transformers.

•

Scenario 87. What is the difference between parametric and non-parametric models?

AnswerParametricNon-parametricExplanation

Answer: - Parametric: Fixed number of parameters regardless of data size (linear regression, neural nets) - Non-parametric: Parameters grow with data (KNN, kernel SVM, decision trees) Explanation: Parametric: compact model, may underfit complex data. Non-parametric: flexible, may overfit, memory grows with data.

•

Scenario 88. What is curriculum learning?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Train on easy examples first, gradually introduce harder examples. Mimics human learning curriculum. Explanation: Can improve convergence speed and final performance. Difficulty can be: loss value, prediction confidence, data complexity. Self-paced learning: model selects its own curriculum.

•

Scenario 89. What is the lottery ticket hypothesis?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Dense neural networks contain sparse subnetworks ("winning tickets") that can achieve comparable performance when trained in isolation from the same initialization. Explanation: Implication: most parameters are unnecessary. Pruning can find these winning tickets. Challenges: finding tickets is expensive (train, prune, rewind, retrain).

•

Scenario 90. What is model pruning?

AnswerTypesUnstructuredStructuredMagnitude pruningExplanation

Answer: Removing unnecessary weights/neurons/layers to create smaller, faster models. Types: 1. Unstructured: Remove individual weights (sparse matrices) 2. Structured: Remove entire neurons/channels/heads (actual speedup) 3. Magnitude pruning: Remove smallest weights Explanation: 90%+ pruning often possible with minimal accuracy loss. Combine with fine-tuning after pruning.

•

Scenario 91. What is quantization for model deployment?

AnswerBenefitsExplanation

Answer: Reducing numerical precision of weights/activations: FP32 → INT8 or even INT4. Benefits: 2-4× memory reduction, 2-4× faster inference, minimal accuracy loss. Explanation: Post-training quantization: quantize after training. Quantization-aware training: simulate quantization during training (better quality). ONNX, TensorRT support quantization.

•

Scenario 92. What is the difference between generative and discriminative models?

AnswerDiscriminativeGenerativeExplanation

Answer: - Discriminative: Learn P(y|x) — decision boundary (Logistic Regression, SVM, Neural Nets for classification) - Generative: Learn P(x,y) or P(x) — data distribution (Naive Bayes, GMM, GANs, VAEs) Explanation: Discriminative: directly model classification boundary. Generative: model how data is generated, can also classify via Bayes' rule.

•

Scenario 93. What is the label smoothing technique?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Replace hard labels [0, 1] with soft labels [ε/K, 1 - ε + ε/K] where ε is typically 0.1 and K is the number of classes. Explanation: Prevents model from being overconfident. Regularization effect. The model can't achieve zero loss → reduces overfitting. Standard in modern image classification and NLP.

•

Scenario 94. What is gradient accumulation?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Accumulate gradients over multiple mini-batches before updating weights. Simulates larger batch size with limited GPU memory.

optimizer.zero_grad()
for i, (x, y) in enumerate(dataloader):
    loss = model(x, y) / accumulation_steps
    loss.backward()
    if (i + 1) % accumulation_steps == 0:
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()

Explanation: 4 batches of 32 with accumulation = effective batch size 128. Essential when model is too large for large batches.

•

Scenario 95. What is the difference between parameters and FLOPs?

AnswerParametersFLOPsExplanation

Answer: - Parameters: Number of learnable weights (determines model size on disk/memory) - FLOPs: Floating-point operations per inference (determines compute cost/speed) Explanation: More parameters ≠ more FLOPs. Attention is O(n²d) FLOPs but O(d²) parameters. MobileNet: fewer FLOPs than VGG but complex architecture.

•

Scenario 96. What is the multi-task learning approach?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Training one model on multiple related tasks simultaneously. Shared representation + task-specific heads.

             → Task Head A (classification)
Shared Backbone
             → Task Head B (regression)

Explanation: Benefits: shared features, regularization effect, data efficiency. Works when tasks are related. Hard task can help easy task and vice versa.

•

Scenario 97. What is contrastive learning?

AnswerLossExplanation

Answer: Learn representations by pulling similar samples together and pushing dissimilar samples apart in embedding space. Loss: contrastive_loss = -log(exp(sim(z_i, z_j)/τ) / Σ exp(sim(z_i, z_k)/τ)) Explanation: SimCLR, MoCo for images. CLIP for image-text. Creates data augmentations, treats augmented versions of same sample as positives, others as negatives.

•

Scenario 98. What is the teacher forcing technique?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: During training of sequence-to-sequence models, use ground truth previous token as input to decoder instead of model's own prediction. Explanation: Without: errors accumulate (exposure bias). With: stable training but mismatch with inference (no ground truth available). Scheduled sampling: gradually shift from teacher forcing to model predictions.

•

Scenario 99. What is the Transformer encoder vs decoder?

AnswerEncoderDecoderEncoder-DecoderExplanation

Answer: - Encoder: Bidirectional self-attention, sees full input. Used for understanding (BERT). - Decoder: Causal (masked) self-attention, sees only past tokens. Used for generation (GPT). - Encoder-Decoder: Encoder processes input, decoder generates output with cross-attention (T5, BART). Explanation: Encoder: classification, NER, semantic search. Decoder: text generation. Encoder-decoder: translation, summarization.

•

Scenario 100. How do you debug a neural network that isn't learning?

AnswerCheck basicsOverfit one batchLearning rateGradientsData

Answer: 1. Check basics: Data loading correct? Labels right? Loss function appropriate? 2. Overfit one batch: If it can't memorize 1 batch, architecture/code is wrong 3. Learning rate: Try 1e-3 (default), or use lr finder 4. Gradients: Check for vanishing/exploding (print gradient norms) 5. Data: Visualize inputs and labels, check preprocessing 6. Simplify: Start with simple model, gradually add complexity 7. Baseline: Compare to known working implementation Explanation: Most training failures are bugs in data loading, preprocessing, or loss computation — not architecture issues. Always overfit one batch first.

Scenario 1. What is the difference between a notebook prototype and a production ML pipeline?

AnswerNotebookProductionExplanation

Answer: - Notebook: Exploratory, manual steps, single execution, no error handling - Production: Automated, reproducible, monitored, scalable, tested, version-controlled Explanation: Notebook → production requires: code refactoring, testing, containerization, monitoring, CI/CD, logging, error handling. ~10× more work than prototyping.

•

Scenario 2. What are the key components of an ML pipeline?

AnswerData ingestionData preprocessingFeature storeTrainingEvaluation

Answer: 1. Data ingestion: Collect, validate incoming data 2. Data preprocessing: Clean, transform, feature engineer 3. Feature store: Store and serve computed features 4. Training: Model training with experiment tracking 5. Evaluation: Validate model performance 6. Registry: Store and version models 7. Serving: Deploy model for inference 8. Monitoring: Track performance, drift, errors Explanation: Each component should be modular, testable, and independently deployable.

•

Scenario 3. What is MLflow and what problems does it solve?

AnswerTrackingProjectsModelsRegistryExplanation

Answer: Open-source ML lifecycle platform: 1. Tracking: Log parameters, metrics, artifacts per experiment 2. Projects: Package code for reproducibility 3. Models: Model packaging and deployment 4. Registry: Model versioning, staging, production transitions Explanation: Without MLflow: manually track experiments in spreadsheets, lose track of best parameters. With MLflow: all experiments logged, comparable, reproducible.

•

Scenario 4. How do you version control ML models?

AnswerCodeDataModelsExperimentsExplanation

Answer: 1. Code: Git for training code, configs, pipelines 2. Data: DVC (Data Version Control), Delta Lake 3. Models: MLflow Model Registry, Weights & Biases 4. Experiments: MLflow tracking, experiment metadata Explanation: Must track: code version + data version + hyperparameters + environment → reproducible model. Code alone is insufficient.

•

Scenario 5. What is a model registry?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Central repository for managing model lifecycle: - Store trained model artifacts - Version models (v1, v2, v3...) - Track model lineage (which data, code, params) - Manage stages: development → staging → production → archived Explanation: MLflow, SageMaker, Vertex AI provide registries. Enables rollback, A/B testing, gradual rollout.

•

Scenario 6. What are the common model serving patterns?

AnswerBatch predictionReal-time APIEdge/embeddedStreamingExplanation

Answer: 1. Batch prediction: Scheduled batch scoring (nightly, hourly) 2. Real-time API: REST/gRPC endpoint for online prediction 3. Edge/embedded: Model deployed on device 4. Streaming: Predictions on data streams (Kafka + model) Explanation: Batch: high throughput, simple. Real-time: low latency requirement. Edge: no network dependency. Choose based on latency requirements and infrastructure.

•

Scenario 7. What is the difference between model serving with REST API vs gRPC?

AnswerRESTgRPCExplanation

Answer: - REST: HTTP/JSON, human-readable, widely compatible, higher latency - gRPC: HTTP/2, Protocol Buffers, binary encoding, lower latency, streaming support Explanation: REST for simplicity and browser compatibility. gRPC for high-performance, low-latency, service-to-service communication. gRPC typically 2-5× faster.

•

Scenario 8. How do you containerize an ML model for deployment?

AnswerExplanation

Answer:

FROM python:3.10-slim
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY model/ /app/model/
COPY serve.py /app/
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["python", "/app/serve.py"]

Explanation: Docker ensures environment consistency. Pin all dependencies. Multi-stage build for smaller images. Use GPU-enabled base images for GPU inference.

•

Scenario 9. What is model drift and how do you detect it?

AnswerData driftConcept driftPrediction driftDetection

Answer: - Data drift: Input feature distribution changes (P(X) shifts) - Concept drift: Relationship between features and target changes (P(Y|X) shifts) - Prediction drift: Output distribution changes Detection: KS test, PSI (Population Stability Index), JS divergence on feature distributions. Monitor prediction distributions over time.

•

Scenario 10. What is the training-serving skew?

AnswerCausesSolution

Answer: Discrepancy between how features are computed during training vs serving. Causes: 1. Different code paths for training and serving 2. Different data sources 3. Different preprocessing logic 4. Feature computation timing differences Solution: Feature store (single source of truth), shared preprocessing code, end-to-end testing.

•

Scenario 11. How do you A/B test ML models in production?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: 1. Split traffic randomly (e.g., 50/50 or 90/10 for canary) 2. Route requests based on user hash (consistent assignment) 3. Measure business metrics (conversion, engagement, revenue) 4. Statistical significance testing before declaring winner 5. Run for sufficient duration (1-4 weeks) Explanation: Never rely on offline metrics alone. A/B test captures real-world impact. Guard rails: monitor latency, error rates.

•

Scenario 12. What is a canary deployment?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Deploy new model to small percentage of traffic (5-10%) and gradually increase if metrics look good.

Day 1: 5% new model, 95% old model
Day 3: 25% new model, 75% old model
Day 7: 50/50
Day 14: 100% new model (if metrics good)

Explanation: Reduces risk of bad deployments. Automatic rollback if key metrics degrade. Shadow mode: run new model on all traffic but only serve old model's predictions.

•

Scenario 13. What is shadow deployment?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Run new model alongside production model on all traffic. New model's predictions are logged but not served. Compare predictions offline. Explanation: Zero risk to users. Validates: latency, error rates, prediction distribution. Limitation: can't measure user behavior impact (only A/B test can).

•

Scenario 14. What is a feature store and why is it important?

AnswerFeaturesTools

Answer: Centralized platform for computing, storing, and serving ML features. Features: 1. Single source of truth for features 2. Share features across models/teams 3. Point-in-time correct feature retrieval (prevents leakage) 4. Online (low-latency) and offline (batch) serving Tools: Feast, Tecton, Hopsworks.

•

Scenario 15. What are the key ML monitoring metrics?

AnswerModel performanceData qualityFeature driftPrediction driftSystem metrics

Answer: 1. Model performance: Accuracy, precision, recall (requires labels) 2. Data quality: Missing values, outliers, schema violations 3. Feature drift: Distribution changes vs training data 4. Prediction drift: Changes in output distribution 5. System metrics: Latency, throughput, error rates, memory Explanation: Labels often delayed → proxy metrics needed. Monitor inputs (drift) as early warning before performance degrades.

•

Scenario 16. How do you handle model retraining?

AnswerTriggersScheduledPerformance-basedData-basedEvent-based

Answer: Triggers: 1. Scheduled: Weekly, monthly, quarterly 2. Performance-based: When monitored metrics drop below threshold 3. Data-based: When significant drift detected 4. Event-based: Known distribution shift (policy change, COVID) Pipeline: Automated data pull → retrain → evaluate → compare vs current model → deploy if better.

•

Scenario 17. What is CI/CD for ML (MLOps)?

AnswerCT (Continuous Training)Explanation

Answer: - CI: Automated testing (unit tests, data validation, model quality tests) on code changes - CD: Automated deployment pipeline (retrain → evaluate → register → deploy) - CT (Continuous Training): Automated retraining on new data Explanation: Unit tests for preprocessing code. Integration tests for pipeline. Model quality tests: performance above threshold. Tools: GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Kubeflow Pipelines.

•

Scenario 18. What tests should you write for ML code?

AnswerUnit testsData validationModel testsIntegration testsPerformance tests

Answer: 1. Unit tests: Individual functions (preprocessing, feature engineering) 2. Data validation: Schema checks, value ranges, missing value rates 3. Model tests: Output shape, probability ranges, deterministic predictions 4. Integration tests: Full pipeline end-to-end 5. Performance tests: Inference latency, throughput Explanation: Test: "Does the model output probabilities between 0 and 1?" "Does preprocessing handle edge cases (empty strings, NaN)?"

Scenario 19. What is ONNX and why is it useful for deployment?

AnswerBenefitsExplanation

Answer: Open Neural Network Exchange — open format for ML models enabling interoperability. Benefits: 1. Framework-agnostic (PyTorch → ONNX → any runtime) 2. ONNX Runtime: optimized inference 3. Hardware-specific optimization (CPU, GPU, edge devices) 4. Typically 2-3× faster inference than native framework Explanation: Train in PyTorch, export to ONNX, serve with ONNX Runtime. Avoids heavy training framework in production.

Scenario 20. How do you handle model latency requirements?

AnswerModel optimizationServing optimizationInfrastructureArchitectureTargets

Answer: 1. Model optimization: Quantization, pruning, distillation 2. Serving optimization: Batching, caching, pre-computation 3. Infrastructure: GPU serving, auto-scaling, CDN for static models 4. Architecture: Simpler model, fewer features, pre-computed embeddings Targets: Real-time search: < 50ms. Recommendation API: < 100ms. Batch scoring: throughput > latency.

Scenario 21. What is model interpretability in production and why does it matter?

AnswerRegulatoryTrustDebuggingBias detectionTools

Answer: 1. Regulatory: GDPR Right to Explanation, Equal Credit Opportunity Act 2. Trust: Users/stakeholders need to understand decisions 3. Debugging: Identify why model makes wrong predictions 4. Bias detection: Ensure model isn't discriminating Tools: SHAP, LIME, feature importance, attention visualization.

AnswerAWS SageMakerGoogle Vertex AIAzure MLDatabricksOpen source

Scenario 23. What is data validation in ML pipelines?

AnswerToolsExplanation

Answer: Automated checks on incoming data:

# Great Expectations example
expect_column_values_to_be_between('age', min=0, max=150)
expect_column_values_to_not_be_null('customer_id')
expect_column_to_exist('purchase_amount')
expect_column_values_to_be_in_set('status', ['active', 'inactive'])

Tools: Great Expectations, TFX Data Validation, Pandera. Explanation: Catch data quality issues before they corrupt model predictions. Run on every data ingestion.

Scenario 24. What is experiment tracking and why is it essential?

AnswerToolsExplanation

Answer: Logging all information about each ML experiment: - Hyperparameters - Metrics (train, validation, test) - Data version - Code version - Environment/dependencies - Artifacts (model, plots, configs) Tools: MLflow, Weights & Biases, Neptune, Comet. Explanation: Without tracking: "Which of the 100 experiments gave the best result?" With tracking: searchable, comparable, reproducible.

Scenario 25. How do you handle model rollback?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: 1. Keep previous model versions in registry 2. Automated rollback trigger (performance drops below threshold) 3. Blue-green deployment (switch back to old model instantly) 4. Feature flags to control model version Explanation: Rollback should be instantaneous — never delete old model before new one is validated. Blue-green: two environments, switch traffic between them.

Scenario 26. What is the difference between online and offline feature computation?

AnswerOffline featuresOnline featuresExplanation

Answer: - Offline features: Computed in batch jobs (daily user aggregates, historical stats) - Online features: Computed in real-time (current session features, real-time events) Explanation: Feature store bridges both: batch features pre-computed and available for low-latency serving. Online features computed at request time.

Scenario 27. What is model governance?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Policies and processes for responsible ML model management: 1. Model documentation (Model Card) 2. Approval workflow for production deployment 3. Audit trail (who deployed what, when) 4. Bias/fairness assessments 5. Performance monitoring requirements 6. Data privacy compliance Explanation: Regulated industries (finance, healthcare) require formal governance. Model Cards document intended use, limitations, and evaluation results.

Scenario 28. What is a Model Card?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Documentation template for ML models including: 1. Model details (architecture, training data) 2. Intended use cases and limitations 3. Performance metrics across subgroups 4. Ethical considerations 5. Maintenance information Explanation: Google introduced Model Cards. Promotes transparency, trust, and responsible ML. Should be updated with each model version.

Scenario 29. How do you ensure reproducibility of ML experiments?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: 1. Set random seeds (Python, NumPy, PyTorch, CUDA) 2. Pin dependency versions (requirements.txt with ==) 3. Version control data (DVC, data snapshots) 4. Log all hyperparameters 5. Container/environment specification (Docker) 6. Store model artifacts with experiment reference Explanation: Full reproducibility: same code + same data + same environment + same random seed → identical model. Often approximated in GPU training due to non-deterministic operations.

Scenario 30. What is the difference between batch inference and real-time inference?

AnswerBatchReal-timeExplanation

Answer: - Batch: Process large dataset at once (hourly/daily), results stored for later retrieval - Real-time: Process single request immediately, return result in milliseconds Explanation: Batch: cost-efficient, higher throughput, doesn't need serving infrastructure. Real-time: requires API, low-latency infrastructure, caching. Many systems use both.

Scenario 33. What is data lineage and why is it important for ML?

AnswerImportanceExplanation

Answer: Tracking the complete journey of data: source → transformations → features → model → predictions. Importance: 1. Debug prediction errors (trace back to source data) 2. Compliance (prove data provenance) 3. Impact analysis (if data source changes, which models affected?) Explanation: Data lineage + model lineage = full traceability. Tools: Apache Atlas, Amundsen, OpenLineage.

Scenario 34. How do you scale ML model serving?

AnswerHorizontal scalingAuto-scalingBatch predictionModel optimizationCaching

Answer: 1. Horizontal scaling: Multiple model replicas behind load balancer 2. Auto-scaling: Scale based on request rate/latency (Kubernetes HPA) 3. Batch prediction: Process many inputs at once 4. Model optimization: Quantization, distillation for faster per-request inference 5. Caching: Cache frequent predictions (Redis, Memcached) Explanation: Start simple (single instance), scale as needed. Kubernetes + auto-scaling handles most production loads.

Scenario 35. What is the difference between model training and model inference optimization?

AnswerTraining optimizationInference optimizationExplanation

Answer: - Training optimization: Faster convergence (optimizer, lr schedule, data loading, distributed training) - Inference optimization: Faster prediction (quantization, pruning, batching, hardware acceleration) Explanation: Training: throughput-oriented, can use large GPUs. Inference: latency-oriented, cost-sensitive, often on cheaper hardware.

Scenario 36. What is TFX (TensorFlow Extended)?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: End-to-end ML platform for production: 1. ExampleGen (data ingestion) 2. StatisticsGen + SchemaGen (data validation) 3. Transform (preprocessing) 4. Trainer (model training) 5. Evaluator (model validation) 6. Pusher (deployment) Explanation: Production-tested at Google. Strong data validation and model analysis. TF-specific but concepts apply universally.

Scenario 37. How do you handle secrets and credentials in ML pipelines?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: 1. Never hardcode in code or configs 2. Environment variables for simple cases 3. Secret managers: AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault 4. Kubernetes Secrets for container deployments Explanation: Database passwords, API keys, cloud credentials must be managed securely. Rotate regularly. Audit access logs.

Scenario 38. What is model compression?

AnswerPruningQuantizationKnowledge distillationLow-rank factorizationArchitecture search

Answer: Techniques to reduce model size for deployment: 1. Pruning: Remove unnecessary weights 2. Quantization: Reduce precision (FP32 → INT8) 3. Knowledge distillation: Train smaller student model 4. Low-rank factorization: Decompose weight matrices 5. Architecture search: Design efficient architectures (MobileNet, EfficientNet) Explanation: Combined: often achieve 10-100× compression with <5% accuracy loss.

Scenario 39. What is concept drift adaptation?

AnswerPeriodic retrainingWindowed trainingOnline learningEnsemble of temporal modelsExplicit drift detection

Answer: Strategies when P(Y|X) changes over time: 1. Periodic retraining: Scheduled model updates 2. Windowed training: Train only on recent data 3. Online learning: Continuous model updates 4. Ensemble of temporal models: Combine models from different time periods 5. Explicit drift detection: DDM, ADWIN algorithms trigger retraining Explanation: Monitor performance metrics. When degradation detected → trigger retraining on recent data. Balance recency and stability.

Scenario 40. How do you implement a feedback loop for ML models?

AnswerExplanation

Answer:

User interaction → Prediction stored → 
Ground truth eventually obtained → 
Performance computed → 
If degraded → Trigger retraining → 
New model evaluated → Deploy if better

Explanation: Feedback can be: explicit (user rates prediction), implicit (user behavior after prediction), or delayed (label becomes available later). Active learning: model requests labels for uncertain predictions.

Scenario 41. What is edge deployment for ML models?

AnswerFrameworksExplanation

Answer: Running models on edge devices (mobile, IoT, browser) instead of cloud servers. Frameworks: TensorFlow Lite (mobile), ONNX Runtime (edge), Core ML (Apple), TensorRT (NVIDIA edge). Explanation: Benefits: low latency, privacy (data stays on device), works offline. Constraints: limited compute, memory, battery.

Scenario 42. What is serverless ML inference?

AnswerLimitationsExplanation

Answer: Run model inference on serverless platforms (AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions) — pay per request, auto-scaling. Limitations: 1. Cold start latency (model loading time) 2. Memory/time limits 3. No GPU (usually) 4. Model size restrictions Explanation: Good for low-traffic, bursty workloads. Pre-warm lambdas for latency-sensitive applications.

Scenario 43. What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling for model serving?

AnswerVerticalHorizontalExplanation

Answer: - Vertical: Bigger machine (more CPU, RAM, GPU) — limited ceiling - Horizontal: More machines/replicas — theoretically unlimited Explanation: Start vertical (simpler). Scale horizontally when hitting limits. Horizontal requires load balancing and stateless design.

Scenario 44. How do you implement model monitoring dashboards?

AnswerToolsExplanation

Answer: 1. Prediction distribution histograms (daily/hourly) 2. Feature value distributions vs training baseline 3. Performance metrics over time (if labels available) 4. Latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) 5. Error rates and types 6. Alerting thresholds for anomalies Tools: Grafana, Datadog, custom dashboards with Streamlit. Explanation: Dashboard must be actionable — alerts should trigger investigation or automatic retraining.

Scenario 45. What is responsible ML deployment?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: 1. Fairness testing across demographic groups 2. Explainability for high-stakes decisions 3. Privacy compliance (GDPR, CCPA) 4. Robustness testing (adversarial, edge cases) 5. Human oversight for critical decisions 6. Fail-safe defaults when model is uncertain Explanation: ML models affect people's lives (loans, hiring, medical diagnosis). Responsible deployment is ethical and legal obligation.

Scenario 46. What is the ML technical debt concept?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Hidden costs that grow over time in ML systems: 1. Data dependencies (unstable upstream data) 2. Configuration dependencies 3. Undeclared consumers of model outputs 4. Pipeline jungles (tangled preprocessing) 5. Dead experimental code Explanation: From Google's "Hidden Technical Debt in ML Systems" paper. ML systems accumulate debt faster than traditional software due to data dependencies.

Scenario 47. How do you handle model fallback strategies?

AnswerFallback modelCached predictionsDegraded serviceCircuit breakerExplanation

Answer: 1. Fallback model: Simple model (rules, heuristics) if primary model fails 2. Cached predictions: Serve last known good prediction 3. Degraded service: Return default/popular items instead of personalized 4. Circuit breaker: Stop sending requests to failing model Explanation: Primary model may fail (timeout, OOM, bug). Fallback ensures service continues. Never return errors to users without trying alternatives.

Scenario 48. What is MLOps maturity model?

AnswerLevel 0Level 1Level 2Explanation

Answer: - Level 0: Manual, ad-hoc (Jupyter notebooks, manual deployment) - Level 1: ML pipeline automation (automated training, manual deployment) - Level 2: CI/CD pipeline automation (automated training + deployment + monitoring) Explanation: Most organizations are Level 0-1. Level 2 requires significant infrastructure investment. Progress incrementally.

Scenario 49. How do you estimate infrastructure costs for ML?

AnswerTrainingServingStorageData processingMonitoring

Answer: 1. Training: GPU hours × cost/hour × retraining frequency 2. Serving: Instances × hours × cost/hour (consider auto-scaling) 3. Storage: Model artifacts + training data + logs 4. Data processing: ETL, feature computation 5. Monitoring: Logging, dashboards, alerting Explanation: GPU training dominates costs for deep learning. Batch inference much cheaper than real-time. Spot instances for training (up to 70% savings).

Scenario 50. What are the key differences between deploying ML in startups vs enterprises?

AnswerStartupEnterpriseExplanation

Answer: - Startup: Move fast, simple infrastructure, cloud-native, few models, one team - Enterprise: Governance, compliance, on-premises/hybrid, many models, cross-team coordination, legacy integration Explanation: Startups: optimize for speed (managed services, simple pipelines). Enterprise: optimize for reliability, security, governance (formal MLOps platform).

Scenario 51. You trained a model with 99.5% accuracy but the stakeholder rejects it. What might be wrong?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: 1. Accuracy misleading due to class imbalance 2. Model doesn't predict the right thing (wrong metric) 3. Latency/cost too high for production 4. Not interpretable enough for regulatory requirements 5. Doesn't handle edge cases important to the business 6. Data leakage gave inflated metrics Explanation: Accuracy alone is insufficient. Understand stakeholder requirements: fairness, explainability, latency, cost, specific error types.

Scenario 52. Your model performs well in development but poorly in production. What are possible causes?

AnswerTraining-serving skewData driftFeature mismatchTime leakageSampling bias

Answer: 1. Training-serving skew: Different preprocessing in train vs serve 2. Data drift: Production data distribution differs from training data 3. Feature mismatch: Features computed differently or missing 4. Time leakage: Used future data in training 5. Sampling bias: Training data not representative of production traffic Explanation: Debug systematically: compare feature distributions, check preprocessing code paths, log predictions vs actuals.

•

Scenario 53. What is Simpson's Paradox and how can it affect ML models?

AnswerExampleExplanation

Answer: A trend that appears in aggregated data reverses when data is split into subgroups. Example: Treatment A has higher overall success rate, but Treatment B is better for EACH disease type when analyzed separately. Explanation: Confounding variable causes this. ML models can learn the confounded pattern. Always check model performance across meaningful subgroups.

•

Scenario 54. You notice your model's performance degrades every Monday. What's happening?

AnswerExplanation

Answer: Likely a day-of-week distribution shift: 1. Different user behavior on Mondays (e.g., higher work-related activity) 2. Data pipeline differences (weekend data batch processed Monday) 3. Seasonal features not capturing weekly patterns Explanation: Add day-of-week features. Train with sufficient weekly variation. Monitor performance by day to catch pattern.

•

Scenario 55. What happens when you train a model on data with label noise?

AnswerMitigationExplanation

Answer: 1. Model learns noise patterns → lower generalization 2. Overparameterized models (deep learning) can memorize noise easily 3. Decision boundary becomes noisy Mitigation: 1. Confident learning (identify noisy labels) 2. Label smoothing 3. Robust loss functions (symmetric cross-entropy) 4. cleanlab library for label noise detection Explanation: Even 5-10% label noise can significantly degrade model performance. Clean data > more data.

•

Scenario 56. How do you handle a scenario where the test set follows a different distribution than training?

AnswerCovariate shift correctionDomain adversarial trainingTransfer learningFeature alignmentExplanation

Answer: Domain adaptation techniques: 1. Covariate shift correction: Importance weighting (weight training samples by P_test(x)/P_train(x)) 2. Domain adversarial training: Learn domain-invariant features 3. Transfer learning: Fine-tune on target domain data 4. Feature alignment: Match feature distributions Explanation: Distribution shift is common (developed country data → developing country deployment). Evaluate on target distribution whenever possible.

•

Scenario 57. What is the trade-off between model complexity and interpretability?

AnswerExplanation

Answer:

Interpretability ←→ Performance
High: Linear Regression, Decision Trees, Rule-based
Medium: Random Forest (with importance), GAMs, EBMs
Low: Deep Learning, XGBoost (to some extent), Neural networks

Explanation: Explainable Boosting Machines (EBMs) and GAMs offer competitive performance with high interpretability. SHAP/LIME can explain any model post-hoc. Regulation may require interpretable models.

Scenario 58. Your Random Forest and XGBoost have identical test performance. Which do you deploy?

AnswerInference speedTraining speedInterpretabilityMaintenanceEdge cases

Answer: Consider: 1. Inference speed: RF is parallelizable (independent trees); XGBoost sequential 2. Training speed: RF faster to train typically 3. Interpretability: Both have feature importance; RF slightly simpler 4. Maintenance: XGBoost has more hyperparameters 5. Edge cases: XGBoost may be more robust to missing values Explanation: If performance is equal, choose the simpler one (Occam's razor). RF is typically simpler to maintain.

Scenario 59. What is Goodhart's Law and how does it apply to ML metrics?

AnswerML exampleExplanation

Answer: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." ML example: Optimizing for click-through rate → model shows clickbait. Optimizing for engagement → model shows outrage. Explanation: Metric hacking: model finds shortcuts to optimize metric without actual improvement. Use multiple metrics, include guardrail metrics, align with business objectives not proxy metrics.

Scenario 60. What is the difference between causation and correlation in ML?

AnswerCorrelationCausationExampleExplanation

Answer: - Correlation: Two variables move together (observed in data) - Causation: One variable directly affects another (requires experimentation or causal inference) Example: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths correlate (both increase in summer). ML might use ice cream to predict drowning — but it's not causal. Explanation: ML models learn correlations. For causal claims: A/B testing, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, causal graphs.

Scenario 61. How do you handle concept drift in a production classification model?

AnswerDetectionAdaptationAlertExplanation

Answer: 1. Detection: Monitor prediction distribution, performance metrics, feature distributions 2. Adaptation: - Retrain on recent data (sliding window) - Online learning (continuous updates) - Ensemble of models from different time periods 3. Alert: Trigger when drift exceeds threshold Explanation: COVID-19 is a dramatic example — consumer behavior shifted overnight, invalidating models trained on pre-COVID data.
